lessons.title: Grammar: Present simple with adverbs of frequency

items.headword: Present simple with adverbs of frequency
items.definition: how to use words like always, usually, and never with the present simple
items.explanationTR:
We use the present simple to talk about habits, routines, and things that are generally true. Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something happens.

Common adverbs of frequency, from 100% to 0%:
• always
• usually
• often
• sometimes
• rarely / hardly ever
• never

Word order:
• Before the main verb: She usually wakes up at seven.
• After the verb 'be': He is always on time.
• 'Sometimes' and 'usually' can also start a sentence: Sometimes I skip breakfast.

Questions with frequency:
• How often do you check your email? — I check it every hour.

Don't forget the regular present simple rules: add -s or -es for he/she/it (she watches, he brushes his teeth), and use don't/doesn't for negatives and do/does for questions. For example: Does she usually cook dinner? No, she doesn't usually cook on weekdays.

purpose.en: Use it for things you do regularly, like your daily routine.
purpose.tr: Düzenli yaptığın şeyler için kullanılır; Türkçedeki "-r" (gelirim, içerim) gibi.

patternNote.en: Add -s only after he, she and it.
patternNote.tr: -s eki sadece he, she ve it'ten sonra gelir.

note.tr: He, she, it varsa fiile -s ekle.

purpose.en: Words like always and never say how often you do something.
purpose.tr: Always (her zaman), usually (genellikle), never (asla) gibi kelimeler bir şeyi ne sıklıkla yaptığını söyler.

patternNote.en: With am, is and are, the word goes after the verb: She is always late.
patternNote.tr: am, is, are ile bu kelime fiilden sonra gelir: She is always late.

examples.en: I always have breakfast at home.
He never watches TV at night.
They are usually tired on Mondays.

mistake.wrong: I go always to work by bus.
mistake.right: I always go to work by bus.

note.en: Put always before the main verb.

explanation.en: "My sister" is she, so the verb takes -s: drinks.
explanation.tr: "My sister" = she; bu yüzden fiile -s gelir: drinks.

questions.prompt: We ---- go to the gym on Saturday mornings.
questions.explanationTR: Adverbs of frequency like "usually" go before the main verb in the present simple ("we usually go"); no form of "be" is needed here because "go" is already the main verb.

questions.prompt: The train ---- late, so I always get to work on time.
questions.explanationTR: With the verb "be," the frequency adverb comes right after "is/am/are" ("is never late"); "never" already means "not ever," so adding "not" or "doesn't" would create a double negative.

questions.prompt: A: ---- do you check your phone in the morning? B: About three times, I think.
questions.explanationTR: "How often" asks about frequency and matches the answer "about three times"; "how much" and "how many" ask about quantity, not frequency.

questions.prompt: He ---- eats vegetables; he only likes pizza and burgers.
questions.explanationTR: "Hardly ever" (almost never) goes before the main verb in the present simple, just like "never" and "rarely"; no extra "does" or "is" is needed in this affirmative sentence.

questions.prompt: ---- I skip breakfast, but most days I eat something small before work.
questions.explanationTR: "Sometimes" is one of the few frequency adverbs that can start a sentence, and it means "occasionally," which fits the contrast with "most days I eat something"; "often," "usually," and "always" would all contradict that contrast.

questions.prompt: My sister ---- to music while she cooks dinner.
questions.explanationTR: Third-person singular subjects like "she" need "-s" on the verb in the present simple ("she usually listens"), and the adverb still goes before the verb.

questions.prompt: I ---- eat fast food; maybe once or twice a year.
questions.explanationTR: "Rarely" already has a negative meaning ("almost never"), so it is not combined with "don't"; it simply goes before the main verb.

questions.prompt: They ---- watch TV after dinner; it's part of their evening routine.
questions.explanationTR: "Always" goes directly before the main verb ("they always watch"); no extra auxiliary like "does" or "is" is needed in this affirmative present simple sentence.

lessons.title: Grammar: Countable and uncountable nouns: some, any, much, many

items.headword: Countable and uncountable nouns: some, any, much, many
items.definition: how to use some, any, much, many, a few, and a little with food nouns
items.explanationTR:
Countable nouns can be counted: one apple, two apples. Uncountable nouns cannot be counted with numbers, like rice, water, and bread; they don't usually have a plural form.

Some and any:
• Use 'some' in positive statements: There is some milk in the fridge. I bought some apples.
• Use 'any' in negatives and questions: There isn't any bread left. Do we have any eggs?

Much and many:
• Use 'many' with countable plural nouns: How many apples do you need? There aren't many eggs left.
• Use 'much' with uncountable nouns: How much milk is in the bottle? There isn't much sugar left.
• In everyday speech, 'a lot of' works with both: a lot of apples, a lot of milk.

A few and a little:
• 'A few' goes with countable nouns: I only have a few carrots.
• 'A little' goes with uncountable nouns: Add a little salt.

Remember: words like bread, rice, water, and information are usually uncountable in English, even when they seem countable in your own language.

questions.prompt: There is ---- juice in the fridge if you're thirsty.
questions.explanationTR: "Some" is used in positive statements; "juice" is uncountable, so "many" and "a few" are wrong, "any" belongs in negatives and questions, and "much" sounds unnatural in a simple positive statement.

questions.prompt: We don't have ---- eggs at all; the carton is empty.
questions.explanationTR: "Any" is used in negative sentences, and "at all" plus "the carton is empty" show there are zero eggs; "many" would suggest a few are left, and "much"/"a little" don't go with the countable noun "eggs."

questions.prompt: ---- apples do we need for the pie?
questions.explanationTR: "Apples" is a countable plural noun, so the question word is "how many"; "how much" is used only for uncountable nouns, and the other forms are not correct English questions.

questions.prompt: ---- sugar do you want in your coffee?
questions.explanationTR: "Sugar" is uncountable, so we ask "how much," not "how many," which is only for countable plural nouns.

questions.prompt: I only have ---- carrots, so I can't make a big salad.
questions.explanationTR: "Carrots" is countable, and "a few" means a small number, matching "can't make a big salad"; "many" would mean a large number, and "much"/"a little" are used only with uncountable nouns.

questions.prompt: There's only ---- rice left, so we should buy more soon.
questions.explanationTR: "Rice" is uncountable, and "a little" means a small amount, matching "we should buy more soon"; "a few" and "many" are used only with countable nouns, and "much" doesn't fit a positive statement like this.

questions.prompt: Would you like ---- coffee?
questions.explanationTR: In friendly offers, we use "some" even in questions ("Would you like some coffee?"); "any" is used in ordinary questions, not offers.

questions.prompt: Could you buy ---- on your way home? We need it for sandwiches.
questions.explanationTR: "Bread" is uncountable, so we say "some bread" (or "a loaf of bread"), not "a bread" or "two breads"; "many" and "a few" go only with countable plural nouns.

items.definition: how to compare two or more things when you shop
items.explanationTR:
When we compare two things, we use the comparative form of an adjective. For short adjectives (one syllable), add -er: cheap becomes cheaper, small becomes smaller. If the adjective ends in a consonant plus -y, change y to i and add -er: easy becomes easier. If it ends in one vowel plus one consonant, double the last letter: big becomes bigger, hot becomes hotter. For longer adjectives (two or more syllables), use more plus the adjective: expensive becomes more expensive, comfortable becomes more comfortable.

When we compare three or more things, we use the superlative form. Add -est for short adjectives, with the word the in front: cheap becomes the cheapest, small becomes the smallest. For longer adjectives, use the most plus the adjective.

• This store is cheaper than that one.
• These shoes are more comfortable than my old ones.
• This is the best shop in the mall.
• That was the most expensive jacket I've ever bought.
• Prices here are lower than online.

A few adjectives are irregular: good becomes better, then the best; bad becomes worse, then the worst. Remember to use than after a comparative (cheaper than) and the before a superlative (the cheapest).

questions.prompt: These jeans are ---- than the ones in the other store.
questions.explanationTR: Cheap is a one-syllable adjective, so the comparative form adds -er: cheaper. "More cheap" is not correct, and "cheapest"/"the cheapest" are superlative forms for three or more things, not for a comparison between two.

questions.prompt: The leather wallet is ---- than the plastic one.
questions.explanationTR: Expensive has three syllables, so its comparative form is more expensive, not expensiver. The superlative forms (most expensive, the most expensive) are used to compare three or more things.

questions.prompt: The service at this store is ---- than at the last one.

questions.prompt: That was ---- sale I've ever seen - nothing was really cheap.

passage.title: Smart Shopping Tips
passage.body:
Shopping can be fun, but it is easy to spend too much money. Here are some simple tips for smart shopping.

First, always make a shopping list before you go to the store. A list helps you buy only the things you really need. Second, compare prices before you buy something expensive, like a phone or a jacket. The same product can be cheaper in a different store or online.

Third, look for sales and discounts, but don't buy something just because it's on sale. Ask yourself: do I really need this? A cheap item is not a bargain if you never use it.

Fourth, keep your receipts. If something breaks or doesn't fit, you can return it or ask for a refund. Most stores will help you if you have the receipt.

Finally, make a budget before you go shopping and try to stay within it. It is easy to spend more than you planned, especially at a big mall with hundreds of stores.

If you follow these tips, you can save money and still buy the things you need.

questions.explanationTR: The text says a cheap item is not a bargain if you never use it. Being on sale or having a discount does not make something a good buy on its own.

lessons.title: Grammar: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs

items.headword: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
items.definition: how to talk about trips and things that happened in the past
items.explanationTR:
We use the past simple to talk about actions that finished in the past, like a trip we took last year.

For regular verbs, add -ed to the base form: arrive becomes arrived, book becomes booked, stay becomes stayed. If the verb ends in -e, just add -d. If it ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add -ed: carry becomes carried. If there is a vowel before the y, just add -ed: stay becomes stayed.

Many common verbs are irregular, so they don't follow this rule. You have to learn their past forms: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, see becomes saw, take becomes took, get becomes got, have becomes had, leave becomes left, fly becomes flew.

• We arrived at the hotel at midnight.
• They flew to Lisbon last summer.
• I bought my ticket online.
• She didn't book a room, so we looked for one at the last minute.
• Did you see the old town?

For negative sentences, use didn't plus the base form: We didn't arrive on time. For questions, use Did plus the subject plus the base form: Did you enjoy the trip?

questions.prompt: We ---- at the airport two hours before our flight.
questions.explanationTR: The trip already happened, so we need the past simple: arrived. "Arrives" and "arriving" are not past forms, and "have arrive" is not a correct verb form.

questions.prompt: Last year, they ---- to Portugal for their vacation.
questions.explanationTR: Fly is irregular, and its past simple form is flew, not flied. "Flown" is the past participle, used with have, not by itself in the past simple.

questions.prompt: I ---- my ticket online last week.
questions.explanationTR: Buy is irregular, and its past simple form is bought. "Buyed" and "boughted" are not real words, and buy/buying are not past forms.

questions.prompt: We ---- a hotel room, so we slept at a friend's house.
questions.explanationTR: Negative past simple sentences use didn't plus the base form: didn't book. After didn't, the verb never takes -ed or -ing.

questions.prompt: ---- you enjoy your trip to Mexico?
questions.explanationTR: Past simple questions use Did + subject + base form: Did you enjoy...? "Do" and "Does" are present tense, and "Were" or "Have" would need a different verb form (enjoying, enjoyed).

questions.prompt: We ---- to the museum on our first day.
questions.explanationTR: Go is irregular, and its past simple form is went, not goed. "Gone" is the past participle, used with have, not alone in the past simple.

questions.prompt: She ---- a lot of photos during the trip.
questions.explanationTR: Take is irregular, and its past simple form is took. "Taken" is the past participle, used with have, and "taked" is not a real word.

questions.prompt: We ---- at a small guesthouse near the beach.
questions.explanationTR: Stay is a regular verb, so its past simple form simply adds -ed: stayed. "Staied" is a spelling mistake, since the y stays after a vowel.

lessons.title: Grammar: There is/are and prepositions of place

items.headword: There is / there are and prepositions of place
items.definition: how to say what exists somewhere and where things are located
items.explanationTR:
We use there is with singular and uncountable nouns, and there are with plural nouns, to say that something exists in a place.
• There is a small park behind our building.
• There are two bathrooms in this apartment.
The negative is there isn't / there aren't, and questions start with Is there...? / Are there...?
• There isn't an elevator, only stairs.
• Are there any shops near your street?
Prepositions of place tell us exactly where something is.
• in / on / at – The keys are on the table. The milk is in the fridge. She's at home.
• next to / between – The bakery is next to the bank. The cafe is between the bakery and the park.
• in front of / behind – There's a bike in front of the door.
• under / above – The cat is sleeping under the bed.
Combine both structures to describe a home or a neighborhood clearly: There is a bus stop in front of our building, and there are two supermarkets between our street and the park.

questions.prompt: ---- a small supermarket at the end of our street.
questions.explanationTR: 'Supermarket' is singular, so the sentence needs 'There is'; 'There are' is used for plural nouns, and 'There has' and 'There be' are not correct forms.

questions.prompt: ---- many old trees in this neighborhood.
questions.explanationTR: 'Trees' is plural, so the sentence needs 'There are'; 'There is' and 'There was' do not agree with a plural noun.

questions.prompt: There ---- a small yard behind the house, but there isn't a garage.
questions.explanationTR: 'Yard' is singular, so 'is' is correct after 'There'; 'are' would need a plural noun, and 'be'/'has'/'having' are not correct here.

questions.prompt: Your keys are ---- the kitchen table, next to the fruit bowl.
questions.explanationTR: 'On' is used for something resting on top of a flat surface like a table; keys 'under' or 'behind' the table could not be next to the fruit bowl.

questions.prompt: Our apartment is ---- the bakery and the pharmacy.
questions.explanationTR: 'Between' is used when something has one thing on each side, here the bakery and the pharmacy; 'next to' only mentions one neighboring place.

questions.prompt: There's a big lamp ---- the dining table; it hangs from the ceiling.
questions.explanationTR: 'Above' means higher than something without touching it, like a lamp that hangs from the ceiling over a table; 'on' would mean the lamp is standing on the table.

questions.prompt: I can't see the TV because my brother is standing right ---- it.

lessons.title: Grammar: Should, must and have to

items.definition: how to give advice and talk about obligation and necessity
items.explanationTR:
We use should to give advice or say what is a good idea. It is not very strong.
• You should drink more water when you have a fever.
• You shouldn't stay up too late if you're sick.
We use must for strong obligation, often rules or something the speaker feels is necessary.
• You must take this medicine three times a day.
• Patients must wash their hands before they enter.
We use have to for obligation that comes from outside, like a rule, a doctor, or a situation.
• I have to see a doctor because my cough isn't getting better.
• She has to rest for a week after the operation.
The negative forms are very different in meaning:
• mustn't means it is forbidden - You mustn't stop taking this medicine suddenly.
• don't have to means it isn't necessary - You don't have to worry; it's not serious.
Must never takes -s or 'to': She must rest (not 'She musts rest' or 'She must to rest'). Have to changes with the subject: I have to, she has to.
Use should for friendly advice, must for strong rules or urgent necessity, and have to for obligations that come from outside you.

questions.prompt: You look tired and you have a headache. Maybe you ---- take a painkiller and rest for a while.
questions.explanationTR: 'Maybe you should...' is a very common way to give friendly advice; 'must' is too strong after 'maybe', and 'mustn't' or 'don't have to' give the wrong meaning.

questions.prompt: This is a hospital rule: all visitors ---- wear a mask in this ward.
questions.explanationTR: 'Must' shows a strict rule that everyone has to follow; 'should' would only be advice, not a hospital rule.

questions.prompt: My cough isn't getting better, so I ---- make an appointment with my doctor.
questions.explanationTR: 'Have to' expresses a necessity caused by the situation, since the cough isn't improving; 'don't have to' would mean it isn't necessary, which contradicts the context.

questions.prompt: The doctor said, "You ---- stop taking this medicine suddenly; it can be dangerous."
questions.explanationTR: 'Mustn't' means it is forbidden, which fits a dangerous action to avoid; 'should' (without 'not') would wrongly recommend stopping suddenly, the opposite of the warning.

questions.prompt: The doctor said the results are fine, so you ---- come back for a follow-up appointment.
questions.explanationTR: 'Don't have to' means coming back isn't necessary, which fits normal results; 'shouldn't' would suggest something negative about returning, which doesn't match good news.

questions.prompt: If the pain doesn't go away tomorrow, I think you ---- call the clinic, just to be safe.
questions.explanationTR: 'Should' fits a personal opinion given as gentle advice, shown by 'I think' and 'just to be safe'; 'have to' and 'must' would state a firm necessity, which is stronger than the sentence intends.

questions.prompt: My brother broke his leg, so he ---- stay at home for six weeks.
questions.explanationTR: With he/she/it, 'have to' becomes 'has to'. 'Must' and 'should' are never followed by 'to', and 'is having' is not used for obligation.

questions.prompt: Because of my allergy, I ---- carry my medicine with me at all times.
questions.explanationTR: 'Have to' shows a necessity that comes from an outside situation, here the allergy; 'don't have to' would mean the opposite, that it isn't necessary.

items.headword: Future plans: going to and present continuous
items.definition: talking about future plans with people using going to and the present continuous
items.explanationTR:
We use two structures to talk about future plans with people we know.

• 'be going to' + base verb describes a plan or intention we have already decided.
  - I'm going to visit my grandparents this weekend.
  - She's going to introduce her boyfriend to the family.

• The present continuous (be + verb-ing) describes a fixed arrangement, often made with another person, usually with a time, day, or place.
  - We're meeting our old classmates for dinner on Friday.
  - He's having lunch with a colleague tomorrow.

The two forms can look similar, but the present continuous usually needs a clear time or place, because it describes something already arranged with someone else. 'Going to' can describe an intention without those details.

• Negative: I'm not going to argue with him again. / They aren't meeting us this week.
• Question: Are you going to apologize to her? / Is she meeting her roommate tonight?

Use 'going to' for plans and for predictions based on what you can see now (Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.), and the present continuous for arrangements already fixed with other people.

questions.prompt: We ---- a big family reunion next Saturday. Everyone has already replied yes.
questions.explanationTR: "Are having" is the present continuous, used here for a fixed future arrangement that people have already confirmed; "were having" is past tense, and the other options are not complete future forms.

questions.prompt: Look at those dark clouds! It ---- soon.
questions.explanationTR: "Is going to rain" makes a prediction based on something we can see right now; "was going to rain" is past tense, and the other options describe the present or the past, not a prediction.

questions.prompt: ---- you meeting your girlfriend's parents next week?
questions.explanationTR: The present continuous question for the subject "you" needs the auxiliary "Are"; the other auxiliaries do not match the -ing verb or the subject.

questions.prompt: My best friend ---- to introduce me to her new colleague at the party tonight.
questions.explanationTR: "Is going to" plus the base verb expresses a plan she has already made; "are going" does not agree with the singular subject, and the other options are missing "is" or are present simple.

questions.prompt: I ---- to apologize to my roommate later today; I already know what I'll say.
questions.explanationTR: "Am going to" agrees with the subject "I" and expresses a plan already decided; "is going" does not agree with "I", and the other forms are not future.

questions.prompt: My parents ---- dinner with our new neighbors this Friday. It's already on the calendar.
questions.explanationTR: The present continuous shows a fixed arrangement that is already on the calendar; "were having" is past, and the other options are not complete future verb forms.

questions.prompt: Are you and your boyfriend ---- in together next month?
questions.explanationTR: After "Are you ...", the present continuous needs the -ing form "moving"; the other options do not complete the continuous structure.

questions.prompt: She isn't ---- her ex-boyfriend to the wedding; they broke up last year.
questions.explanationTR: The negative present continuous "isn't inviting" needs the -ing form; the other options do not fit correctly after "isn't".

passage.title: An Email from a Friend
passage.body:
Hi Maria,

I hope you're doing well! I have so much news to share with you.

First, I moved to a new apartment last month. My new roommate is really friendly, and we get along very well. She's honest and generous, and she always helps me when I'm stressed about work.

Second, do you remember Daniel from university? We kept in touch after graduation, and now we're dating! He's going to introduce me to his family next weekend, so I'm a little nervous. He's very patient with me, though, and I feel confident when I'm with him.

I also have some sad news. My colleague Sofia broke up with her boyfriend after five years together. They still get along, but it wasn't an easy decision. I'm going to invite her out for coffee this week so she isn't alone.

What about you? Are you still single, or is there someone new in your life? I know your last relationship ended badly, but I'm sure you'll find someone who deserves you.

Let's keep in touch more often. Maybe we can meet up next month?

Love,
Elena

We often use 'ever' in questions and 'never' in negative sentences.
• Have you ever taken a cooking class?
• He has never been good at knitting.

When we know exactly when something happened, we use the past simple instead.
• I have visited that hiking trail. (an experience, no specific time)
• I visited that hiking trail last summer. (a specific time)

'Just', 'already', and 'yet' often appear with the present perfect: She has already tried gardening. Have you finished your painting yet?

Remember to use the past participle after have/has, not the past simple form (has gone, not has went). Common irregular participles: be → been, see → seen, take → taken, do → done. Use 'been' for places you visited and came back from: I have been to Japan.

questions.prompt: ---- you ever tried painting?
questions.explanationTR: "Have" combines with "you" and the past participle to ask about a life experience; "Did" would need the past simple, and the other auxiliaries don't fit this structure.

questions.prompt: I ---- never been hiking in the mountains.
questions.explanationTR: The subject "I" takes "have" in the present perfect; "has" is for he/she/it, and the other options are not present perfect forms.

questions.prompt: She ---- tried many different hobbies this year.
questions.explanationTR: The subject "she" needs "has" in the present perfect; "have" is for I/you/we/they, and the other options are not present perfect.

questions.prompt: Have you ---- taken a cooking class before?
questions.explanationTR: "Ever" is used in present perfect questions asking about life experience; "yet" and "already" fit different kinds of sentences, and "never" is for negative statements.

questions.prompt: He has ---- been good at knitting; he always struggles with it.
questions.explanationTR: "Never" shows an experience that hasn't happened, matching "always struggles"; the other adverbs don't fit a negative experience.

questions.prompt: I ---- that hiking trail last summer.
questions.explanationTR: "Last summer" is a specific past time, so the past simple "visited" is correct; the present perfect options don't fit a stated specific time.

questions.prompt: She has already ---- her painting; you can see it now.
questions.explanationTR: After "has already", we need the past participle "finished"; the other forms do not complete the present perfect correctly.

questions.prompt: My brother loves hiking. He has ---- to the mountains in Nepal three times.
questions.explanationTR: "Been" is the past participle we use for visits and experiences ("has been to"); "went" is the past simple and can't follow "has", and "go", "being" and "was" are not past participles.

passage.title: A Hobby That Changed My Life
passage.body:
Five years ago, I was often stressed and bored after work. I didn't have any hobbies, and my free time felt empty. Then a colleague invited me to try hiking with her group on weekends.

At first, I wasn't very good at it. I felt nervous during the first trip because the trail was long and difficult. But I didn't give up. I kept practicing, and soon I started to enjoy the fresh air and the quiet mountains.

After a few months, I noticed a big change. I felt calmer and happier, even at work. I also made new friends in the hiking group, and we keep in touch every week. Hiking gave me something to look forward to, and it taught me to be more patient with myself.

Last year, I finally achieved a goal I never thought possible: I hiked to the top of a real mountain. I have never felt so proud. Now I encourage my friends to take up a hobby, too. It doesn't matter what hobby you choose — the important thing is to try something new and give it time. You might discover a talent you never knew you had.
